trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), a single next_token() walk, get_token_type()/get_tag() to identify SPAN tag tokens, and serialize_token() to build normalized rewritten output. All called methods are documented in the rendered files and no _doing_it_wrong records occurred. Minor issue: the raw-input fallback on create_fragment() failure or get_last_error() would not satisfy a normalized rewritten-output contract if reached.

Correct processor and documented API surface throughout, including documented WP_HTML_Processor::normalize(). The main loop is idiomatic and matches the serialize_token() rewrite pattern. The weakness is the fallback: normalize($html) after a token rewrite is specifically warned about because it restarts from the original bytes and would discard skipped SPAN tokens if that branch were reached.

Uses the intended HTML Processor fragment parser and the canonical token-serialization rewrite pattern. All methods are documented, and no misuse was reported. Minor edge-policy gap: it returns raw input if processor creation fails and never checks get_last_error(), so unsupported-parser aborts could produce a partial rewrite rather than an explicit fallback.

failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all three passed 7/7. The docs appear to have succeeded because the HTML Processor overview explicitly says to use it for structure and normalized output, create_fragment() matches body-fragment input, next_token() explains that walks see text plus opening and closing tokens including virtual closers, and serialize_token() directly documents the needed rewrite pattern: concatenate serialized tokens, skip tokens to remove them, and skip closers too. The serialize_token() section’s analogous SUP-removal example likely prevented the common mistakes of using get_updated_html(), using next_tag() without closers, or rebuilding text manually. Near-misses were limited to fallback semantics: candidates still wrote raw-input or normalize-original fallbacks, even though the docs warn those discard the accumulated rewrite. The unclosed-span case was handled because an unclosed element is virtually closed and serialized; it is not the same as a truncated/incomplete syntax token.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that raw input and normalize($html) discard a rewrite, but candidates still used those as fallbacks in string-returning rewrite functions.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short contract-oriented note: for functions promising normalized rewritten HTML, returning raw input or normalize($html) is not equivalent to returning the rewrite; choose accumulated best-effort output, null/empty failure, or another explicit documented policy.

doc_gaps.problem: The distinction between an unclosed element that receives a virtual closer and a truly incomplete trailing syntax token is easy to miss.

doc_gaps.problem: Element-token filtering depends on knowing that tag closers are also '#tag' tokens and get_tag() returns the same tag name for opener and closer.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State explicitly in get_tag() or get_token_type() that opener and closer tag tokens both report '#tag' and the tag name; use is_tag_closer() only when the opener/closer distinction matters.
